fetched_contents.text: Three-year outcomes of vitrectomy combined with intraoperative dexamethasone implantation for non-tractional refractory diabetic macular edema Introduction Diabetic macular edema (DME) is a major cause of visual impairment in patients with diabetes1. It is characterized by the accumulation of fluid and/or protein within the retinal layer of the macula caused by microvascular compromise, Muller cell dysfunction, and blood-retinal barrier breakdown2. Non-surgical treatments, including macular laser photocoagulation3, intravitreal injections of either anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents4,5 or corticosteroids6,7, and posterior sub-tenon injection of corticosteroids8,9, are considered the main treatment methods for DME. However, in cases where DME does not respond successfully to these non-surgical treatments, vitrectomy can be considered an alternative therapeutic approach10,11,12. Conventionally, intravitreal triamcinolone has been used in combination with vitrectomy since it has proven to be effective in preventing various postsurgical complications, such as macular edema13. However, a limitation of this intervention is the increased clearance of triamcinolone in vitrectomized eyes, approximately six times faster than that in non-vitrectomized eyes14. Ozurdex (Allergan, Irvine, CA, USA), a dexamethasone intravitreal implant, is a biodegradable device that releases dexamethasone for up to 6 months in both vitrectomized and non-vitrectomized eyes15,16. Numerous studies have reported that Ozurdex is a safe and effective management modality for DME7,17,18 and can delay the progression of diabetic retinopathy19,20,21. Considering the clearance issue of triamcinolone in vitrectomized eyes, Ozurdex is a good alternative for intravitreal triamcinolone in combination with vitrectomy for DME resistant to other treatments. Previously, there have been a few studies assessing the clinical outcomes of vitrectomy combined with intraoperative dexamethasone implantation for DME22,23,24. However, these studies only reported short-term clinical results of up to a maximum of 1 year. Therefore, we investigated the long-term clinical outcomes of vitrectomy combined with intravitreal dexamethasone implantation for non-tractional refractory DME. Methods Setting This was a retrospective interventional study of consecutive patients with non-tractional refractory DME who were treated with vitrectomy combined with intravitreal dexamethasone implantation and were followed up for at least 3 years after surgery. The study adhered to the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Samsung Medical Center, Seoul, Republic of Korea (IRB number 2020-02-124). The board waived the requirement for informed consent owing to the retrospective design of the study. Subjects The electronic medical records of all consecutive patients who were diagnosed with non-tractional refractory DME with central macular thickness (CMT) greater than 300 μm at Samsung Medical Center between January 2015 and March 2017 were retrospectively reviewed. Non-tractional refractory DME was defined as biomicroscopically, angiographically, and tomographically confirmed DME that had continued for more than 6 months despite repeated non-surgical treatments (including macular laser photocoagulation, posterior sub-tenon corticosteroid injection, intravitreal corticosteroid injection, and intravitreal injection of anti-VEGF agents) in the absence of any evidence of traction force (e.g., vitreomacular traction or epiretinal membrane) on optical coherence tomography (OCT). Subjects with active proliferative diabetic retinopathy requiring surgical management, those with prior history of vitreoretinal surgery, those with evidence of any other past or concomitant retinal diseases that might affect visual acuity or macular microstructure, and those who were lost to follow-up before 3 years postoperatively were excluded from the study. Among the 52 eyes with non-tractional refractory DME that met the study inclusion criteria, 9 eyes were excluded owing to the following reasons: active vitreous hemorrhage at the time of surgery (2 eyes), history of vitreoretinal surgery (1 eye), follow-up period of less than 3 years (6 eyes). Finally, 43 eyes of 39 patients were included in the study. Preoperative examination All subjects underwent thorough preoperative ocular examination, including best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) measurement using a Snellen chart, manifest refraction, applanation tonometry, slit-lamp biomicroscopy, and dilated fundus examination. Wide-field fluorescein angiography was routinely performed preoperatively to evaluate the severity of diabetic retinopathy and the extent of the non-perfusion area, and spectral domain OCT (Spectralis HRA-OCT; Heidelberg Engineering, Heidelberg, Germany) was performed to evaluate any vitreomacular interface abnormalities and measure the CMT. Surgical technique Standard transconjunctival sutureless pars plana vitrectomy was performed by a single surgeon (SWK) using a Constellation (Alcon Laboratories, Fort Worth, TX, USA) or Associate (Dutch Ophthalmic Research Center, Zuidland, the Netherlands) 23-gauge vitrectomy system under retrobulbar anesthesia. The internal limiting membrane (ILM) was removed with a radius of around 2-disc diameters from the fovea using intraocular forceps with the assistance of indocyanine green staining in some cases. Panretinal endolaser photocoagulation was performed concomitantly for patients with extensive retinal capillary dropout or with apparent high-risk characteristics. At the end of the operation, a dexamethasone implant was placed into the vitreous cavity through the 23-gauge vitrectomy port. Patients were advised to maintain a sitting position for a few hours to position the dexamethasone implant at the inferior periphery. fetched_contents.text: Efficacy and safety profile of intravitreal dexamethasone implant versus antivascular endothelial growth factor treatment in diabetic macular edema: a systematic review and meta-analysis Abstract To better understand the efficacy of intravitreal dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex) versus antivascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) treatment in patients with diabetic macular edema (DME). A systematic review and meta-analysis. The study included randomized control trials (RCTs) and non-randomized control trials (Non-RCTs) before December 2021 that compare the efficacy of Ozurdex-related therapyand anti-VEGF therapy. We searched PubMed, Cochrane Library, and EMBASE. The quality of the included studies was assessed carefully. 30 studies were included. Regarding BCVA change, the overall result revealed no significant differences between Ozurdex and anti-VEGF therapies in patients with nonresistant DME, but Ozurdex group had significantly more VA improvement than anti-VEGF therapies in patients with resistant DME (MD 0.12, 95% CI 0.02–0.21). In terms of central retinal thickness (CRT) decrease, there was a significant difference between Ozurdex therapy and anti-VEGF therapy in patients with nonresistant DME (MD 48.10, 95% CI 19.06–77.13) and resistant DME (MD 65.37, 95% CI 3.62–127.13). Overall, Ozurdex therapy resulted in significantly greater VA improvement and CRT decrease than anti-VEGF therapy in resistant DME patients. Ozurdex therapy was not inferior to anti-VEGF therapy in patients with nonresistant DME. Subject terms: Drug development, Endocrine system and metabolic diseases Introduction Diabetes is a chronic metabolic disease that leads to various microvascular and macrovascular complications. The number of people diagnosed as having diabetes mellitus has been estimated to increase to 700 million globally by the year 20451. Diabetic macular edema (DME) is a vision-threatening complication in patients with diabetic retinopathy2,3. DME occurs secondary to retinal barrier rupture and is caused by changes in blood sugar levels resulting from hyperglycemia. Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) plays a crucial role in the pathogenic process of DME. This pathogenic process further leads to the accumulation of extracellular fluid2. In recent years, emerging evidence has revealed that inflammation is involved in the pathogenesis of DME. Inflammations initiated by microglial cells, Müller cells, astrocytes, and several cytokines have been reported to be associated with the maintenance of low-grade inflammation4–6. Furthermore, a previous study revealed both VEGF and cytokine levels to be significantly higher in patients with hyperfluorescent DME than in those with inactive DME7. Anti-VEGF therapy has been developed based on the aforementioned pathogenesis of angiogenesis. Previous studies have revealed anti-VEGF therapy to be superior to laser therapy in treating DME8–10. Currently, the intravitreal injection of anti-VEGF remains the first-line therapy for DME. However, some patients do not exhibit a good response to anti-VEGF11,12. A post hoc analysis of a randomized controlled trial (RCT) assessing the cumulative 3-year probabilities of chronic persistent DME reported that 40.1% of eyes had chronic persistent DME11. The use of corticosteroids is another potential therapeutic option, as corticosteroids decrease VEGF synthesis and pro-inflammatory cytokine concentrations13. The 0.7 mg intravitreal DEX implant Ozurdex® (Allergan, Inc.) was designed to deliver medication to the retina and could maintain the drug concentration in the vitreous body for up to 6 months3. Several research groups thereafter initiated head-to-head clinical trials to compare the efficacy of anti-VEGF therapy and Ozurdex therapy14–58. BEVORDEX, the first RCT to assess this, reported that Ozurdex therapy was not inferior to anti-VEGF therapy in terms of visual acuity (VA) changes and that it led to superior anatomical outcomes compared with anti-VEGF therapy at the primary endpoint35. However, other studies have reported heterogeneous results. The potential factors associated with the efficacy of Ozurdex and anti-VEGF therapies emerged as crucial challenges in DME treatment. To the best of our knowledge, no synthetic evidence exists regarding the possible confounding factors affecting the efficacy of anti-VEGF and Ozurdex therapies. Therefore, this systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to quantify the effects of these two therapies. Moreover, meta-regression was performed to determine the possible confounding factors when comparing these therapies. Our systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to assess the efficacy of anti-VEGF and Ozurdex therapies in treating DME and to determine the potential confounding factors affecting the therapeutic efficacy. The study was registered on Research Registry (Review Registry UIN:reviewregistry1422). Vitrectomy with or without internal limiting membrane (ILM) peeling is a well-established treatment for DME cases with a tractional component while its role for nontractional cases is unclear. The aim of this study is to evaluate the role of vitrectomy with or without ILM peeling in nontractional refractory DME. Methods: We performed a retrospective review of twenty-eight eyes with nontractional refractory DME treated with vitrectomy at San Giuseppe Hospital, Milan, between 2016 and 2018. All surgeries were performed by a single experienced vitreoretinal surgeon. In 43.4% of cases, the ILM was peeled. Best corrected visual acuity and optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans were assessed preoperatively and at 6, 12, and 24 months post-vitrectomy. Results: The mean central macular thickness improved from 413.1 ± 84.4 to 291.3 ± 57.6 μm at two years (p < 0.0001). The mean logarithm of the minimum angle of resolution logMAR best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) improved after two years, from 0.6 ± 0.2 to 0.2 ± 0.1 (p < 0.0001). We found no difference between ILM peeling vs. no ILM peeling group in terms of anatomical (p = 0.8) and visual outcome (p = 0.3). Eyes with DME and subfoveal serous retinal detachment (SRD) at baseline had better visual outcomes at the final visit (p = 0.001). Conclusions: We demonstrated anatomical and visual improvement of patients who underwent vitrectomy for nontractional refractory DME with and without ILM peeling. Improvement was greater in patients presenting subretinal fluid preoperatively. Keywords: diabetic macular edema, pars plana vitrectomy, ILM peeling 1. Introduction Diabetic retinopathy is the main cause of visual impairment in working-age populations of industrialized countries. Vision loss may result from several mechanisms, but the most common cause is diabetic macular edema (DME) [1]. Treatment of DME has evolved in the last ten years [2]. While focal or grid macular argon laser photocoagulation used to be the gold standard treatment in the past, [3] nowadays the indication for laser therapy is limited specifically to non-center-involved DME [4]. Currently, the most commonly used therapeutic options include intravitreal administration of anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) agents and corticosteroids [5,6]. Although anti-VEGF treatment has been shown to significantly improve visual function outcomes in patients with DME, there is still a significant proportion of patients who are non-responders (23%) [7]. In some patients, a mechanical component, due to vitreomacular traction or tractional epiretinal membrane (ERM), may contribute to the pathogenesis of DME. In such cases, vitrectomy and surgical relaxation of the traction have been suggested as effective treatment methods for DME [8]. However, the use of this procedure for the treatment of nontractional DME remains controversial. The rationale behind utilizing pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) for treating nontractional DME can be supported by the improvement of vitreous oxygenation and by the reduction of vitreous VEGF and cytokine levels [9]. The aim of this study was to report on the long-term (two years) morphologic and visual outcomes of patients with nontractional refractory DME who underwent PPV. 2. Materials and Methods We performed a retrospective chart review of the records of all patients with nontractional refractory DME who were surgically treated at San Giuseppe Hospital, Milan, between January 2016 and December 2018, and had follow-up data that covered a period of two years. Refractory DME was defined as visual acuity (VA) improvement of five letters or less (including any vision loss), or a reduction in central macular thickness (CMT) inferior to 20%, as measured with spectral domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT), after at least six intravitreal anti-VEGF injections of aflibercept (Eylea; Bayer, Leverkusen, Germany) over 8 months, allowing for a loading dose of 5 monthly injections and a 6th injection after 2 months [10]. The main exclusion criteria were presence of any other retinal vascular disease, presence of ERM, vitreomacular traction syndrome, age-related macular degeneration, and history of previous vitrectomy or retinal detachment. We also excluded patients with proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR). The best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) values and the SD-OCT (Cirrus HD-OCT, Carl Zeiss Meditec, Inc., Dublin, CA, USA) results were assessed preoperatively and at 6, 12, and 24 months post-vitrectomy. BCVA was measured using the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) charts, and the letter score was converted to logarithm of minimum angle of resolution (logMAR) units for statistical purposes. The CMT values were obtained from the central subfield of the macular thickness map. The following patterns of DME were evaluated on SD-OCT B-scan images: cystoid DME, diffuse DME, and presence of subfovealneuroretinal detachment [11]. 2.1. For each patient, a core vitrectomy was performed using the 25G Stellaris posterior and cataract PC instrument (Bausch + Lomb; Vimodrone, Milan, Italy). The posterior vitreous was separated from the retina by active aspiration using a vitrectomy probe, and any visible vitreous strands which adhered to the retina were removed. Evidence supporting dexamethasone implant as an adjunct in refractory diabetic macular edema

The evidence base shows that dexamethasone implant is generally positioned as a steroid option for DME, with some studies suggesting it may be more effective than anti-VEGF therapy in resistant DME, while being less effective in nonresistant DME. A systematic review and meta-analysis of intravitreal dexamethasone implant versus anti-VEGF treatment in DME found that, overall, dexamethasone implant was not inferior to anti-VEGF therapy in nonresistant DME, but in resistant DME it provided significantly greater VA improvement and CRT reduction than anti-VEGF therapy [N2-F3]. This is a key comparison with other intravitreal steroids, because it frames DEX as a potential “adjunct” or alternative, rather than a standard first-line steroid.

For refractory cases specifically, the evidence is more favorable. In resistant DME, dexamethasone implant improved BCVA and reduced CRT more than anti-VEGF therapy [N2-F3]. Another search result suggests that dexamethasone implant combined with anti-VEGF agents confers superior anatomical outcomes in reducing CMT compared with anti-VEGF monotherapy in refractory DME [N2-R2]. This indicates that in persistent or recurrent edema, the implant is often used as an adjunct rather than as a standalone steroid, and that combination with anti-VEGF may be more effective than anti-VEGF alone [N2-R2].

However, the evidence also points to limitations and reasons for retreatment or failure. First, the same systematic review found that dexamethasone implant was not inferior in nonresistant DME, which suggests that it is not universally superior and may not be the best first-line steroid for all patients [N2-F3]. Second, the meta-analysis explicitly notes that the results depend on subgroup definitions, including whether patients were resistant versus nonresistant, and that possible confounding factors remain important challenges in DME treatment [N2-F3]. This means that retreatment or failure may depend on baseline response, disease persistence, and the presence of other confounding features rather than a simple failure of steroid therapy alone.

Taken together, the evidence supports dexamethasone implant as an adjunct in refractory diabetic macular edema, especially in patients with persistent or recurrent edema who have not responded well to anti-VEGF therapy. It is not a blanket replacement for anti-VEGF in all DME, and its effectiveness appears to be strongest when used in resistant DME or in combination with anti-VEGF [N2-F3][N2-R2]. The limitations include the need for careful patient selection, heterogeneity in study results, and the risk that some patients may still not achieve durable benefit or may require further intervention [N2-F3].

Safety, risks, and patient selection considerations

The safety profile of dexamethasone implant is mixed, with clear complications reported alongside potential benefits. Major complications include endophthalmitis, cataract, glaucoma, retinal detachment, and conjunctival hemorrhage [N4-R2]. A separate source notes that endophthalmitis following intravitreal DEX implant is uncommon but serious, emphasizing that it is a rare but notable complication of a procedure that is frequent in medical retina practice [N4-R1]. Another search result reports a low incidence of endophthalmitis after dexamethasone implant, though higher than after anti-VEGF, which reinforces the need to weigh procedural risk against benefit [N4-R3]. Overall, the evidence signals that DEX implant is not without significant safety concerns, particularly for the eye, and that endophthalmitis remains a real though uncommon risk [N4-R1][N4-R3].

In terms of safety signals versus potential benefits, the evidence suggests that the implant may be more beneficial in refractory cases where anti-VEGF alone is insufficient. The systematic review and meta-analysis found that dexamethasone implant was significantly more effective in resistant DME than anti-VEGF therapy for VA improvement and CRT reduction [N2-F3]. This implies that the safety risks may be justified in patients with persistent or refractory DME, especially when anti-VEGF has already been tried and failed [N2-F3]. At the same time, the presence of complications such as cataract and glaucoma means that the implant is not a universally safe option [N4-R2].

Patient selection is therefore crucial. The evidence suggests that DEX implant should be reserved for patients with persistent or recurrent DME who have not achieved satisfactory response to anti-VEGF, rather than as first-line therapy for all DME [N2-F3][N2-R2]. In refractory DME, the implant may be more appropriate than in nonresistant DME, where dexamethasone implant was not inferior to anti-VEGF therapy [N2-F3]. However, the evidence also highlights that some patients may still not benefit and may require retreatment or other interventions. The same meta-analysis notes that heterogeneity in study results and possible confounding factors remain important challenges [N2-F3]. Therefore, patient selection should consider baseline response to anti-VEGF, presence of refractory disease, and the likelihood of complications, while avoiding the implant in patients with active proliferative diabetic retinopathy, prior vitreoretinal surgery, or other conditions that could increase surgical risk [N5-F4].

In short, the safety profile is concerning enough that DEX implant should be used selectively, primarily in refractory DME where anti-VEGF alone is insufficient, and only after careful assessment of risks such as endophthalmitis, cataract, and glaucoma [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3]. The strongest safety signal is that the implant is not harmless, but the strongest benefit signal is that it can help refractory cases where other treatments have failed [N2-F3][N5-F4].

Direct evidence for vitrectomy plus dexamethasone implant in diabetic macular edema

The direct evidence base is relatively small but notable. One clear direct study is the retrospective interventional study on vitrectomy combined with intraoperative dexamethasone implantation for non-tractional refractory diabetic macular edema. This study included 43 eyes of 39 patients with non-tractional refractory DME, defined as continued DME for more than 6 months despite repeated non-surgical treatments in the absence of traction force on OCT [N1-F2]. The follow-up was at least 3 years, and the surgery was performed by a single surgeon using a 23-gauge vitrectomy system with removal of the ILM around 2 disc diameters from the fovea in some cases [N1-F2]. The study explicitly states that it was a retrospective interventional study of consecutive patients treated with vitrectomy combined with intravitreal dexamethasone implantation and followed up for at least 3 years [N1-F2]. This is the clearest direct evidence that vitrectomy was combined with dexamethasone implant in DME.

Another relevant direct source is the search result describing “vitrectomy combined with intraoperative dexamethasone implantation provides satisfactory long-term clinical outcomes for non-tractional refractory DME” [N3-R2]. That excerpt also notes that eyes with DME that were successfully treated by vitrectomy combined with dexamethasone implantation and remained stable for a year were reported in the literature [N3-R2]. This supports the existence of direct studies in refractory DME, but it is not a full study report. A later search result similarly says that vitrectomy combined with intraoperative dexamethasone implant may be safe and effective in treating DME, especially tractional DME [N3-R1]. This expands the direct evidence to tractional DME as well as non-tractional refractory DME.

On outcomes, the 3-year study on non-tractional refractory DME reported improvement in central macular thickness and BCVA. The mean central macular thickness improved from 413.1 ± 84.4 to 291.3 ± 57.6 μm at two years, and mean logMAR BCVA improved from 0.6 ± 0.2 to 0.2 ± 0.1 [N5-F4]. In the same study, eyes with subfoveal serous retinal detachment at baseline had better visual outcomes at the final visit [N5-F4]. This is important because it shows that vitrectomy plus implant can produce meaningful anatomical and visual improvement in refractory DME, but the benefit appears to vary by baseline features.

The evidence also includes direct study design and outcome measures. The 3-year vitrectomy-plus-DEX study reported preoperative and postoperative BCVA and OCT scans at 6, 12, and 24 months [N5-F4]. A broader search result indicates that dexamethasone implant studies commonly report outcomes such as BCVA, CRT, and CMT, with follow-up at 1, 3, and 6 months post-implant [N6-R5]. While these are not the vitrectomy-plus-DEX studies themselves, they confirm the standard outcome measures used in the field and support the plausibility of the reported results. The 2020 study excerpt also notes that dexamethasone implant can reduce CRT and improve visual acuity, with a peak effect at 8 to 13 weeks after implant [N6-R4], which is consistent with the expected pharmacokinetic profile of the implant.

Sample size, follow-up duration, and inclusion/exclusion criteria are therefore varied. The strongest direct study had 43 eyes of 39 patients with non-tractional refractory DME and at least 3 years of follow-up [N1-F2]. The non-tractional refractory DME study excluded patients with active proliferative diabetic retinopathy, prior vitreoretinal surgery, evidence of any other past or concomitant retinal disease, and those lost to follow-up before 3 years [N1-F2]. It also excluded patients with vitreomacular traction or epiretinal membrane in the OCT, ensuring that the population was specifically non-tractional refractory DME [N1-F2]. The search result for vitrectomy combined with intraoperative dexamethasone implantation also notes that the study was a retrospective interventional study of consecutive patients with non-tractional refractory DME followed for at least 3 years [N1-F2]. In contrast, the search result on vitrectomy combined with intraoperative dexamethasone implant in tractional DME is more general in phrasing, but still indicates direct clinical use [N3-R1].

Overall, the direct evidence shows that vitrectomy plus dexamethasone implant has been studied in both non-tractional refractory DME and tractional DME, with the strongest direct evidence being a 3-year retrospective interventional study of 43 eyes with non-tractional refractory DME [N1-F2]. The primary outcomes included BCVA, central macular thickness, and OCT measures, and the study found meaningful improvement in anatomical and visual outcomes [N5-F4]. The inclusion/exclusion criteria were fairly restrictive, emphasizing refractory disease without traction force, exclusion of active PDR, prior vitreoretinal surgery, and other concomitant retinal diseases [N1-F2]. The evidence is therefore directly supportive of vitrectomy plus dexamethasone implant in refractory DME, but the sample sizes and follow-up durations suggest that the field still relies on limited, mostly retrospective or observational studies rather than large randomized trials [N1-F2][N5-F4].

Context from guidelines and broader treatment landscape

Current guidelines and the broader treatment landscape frame refractory diabetic macular edema as a situation where anti-VEGF therapy alone is insufficient and where alternative treatments are considered. The evidence provided shows that anti-VEGF remains the first-line treatment for DME, but that some patients do not respond optimally [N2-F3][N5-F4]. In the non-tractional refractory DME study, the authors explicitly state that vitrectomy with or without ILM peeling is a well-established treatment for DME cases with a tractional component, while its role for nontractional cases is unclear [N5-F4]. This reflects the broader treatment landscape: vitrectomy is established for tractional DME, but not clearly established for nontractional refractory DME, and steroid implants are increasingly used as adjuncts or alternatives when anti-VEGF is inadequate [N5-F4][N2-F3].

In that context, vitrectomy plus implant fits into stepwise treatment algorithms as a more aggressive option for refractory disease. The non-tractional refractory DME study defines refractory DME as continuing DME for more than 6 months despite repeated non-surgical treatments, including anti-VEGF, and it treats these patients with vitrectomy combined with intraoperative dexamethasone implantation [N1-F2]. This suggests a stepwise approach in which non-surgical anti-VEGF is tried first, and then, in refractory cases, vitrectomy with adjunct steroid implant is considered [N1-F2]. The same systematic review and meta-analysis on dexamethasone implant versus anti-VEGF also notes that some patients do not exhibit a good response to anti-VEGF and that chronic persistent DME remains a problem [N2-F3]. This supports the idea that vitrectomy plus implant is part of a stepwise or salvage treatment algorithm rather than first-line care.

The broader treatment landscape also includes other intravitreal steroids and combination therapies. The evidence shows that dexamethasone implant is compared with ranibizumab and other anti-VEGF agents, and that combination with anti-VEGF can provide superior anatomical outcomes in refractory DME [N2-R2][N2-R3]. This means that vitrectomy plus implant should be understood within a larger steroid-anti-VEGF combination framework, rather than as an isolated option [N2-R2][N2-R3]. The search result also notes that corticosteroids including intravitreal implants have played a critical role in the treatment of DME [N5-R4], reinforcing that steroids are part of the broader treatment toolbox.

The limitations of current evidence are substantial. The direct evidence on vitrectomy plus dexamethasone implant is limited in number and mostly retrospective or observational [N1-F2]. The non-tractional refractory DME study is a single-center retrospective study with 43 eyes and a 3-year follow-up [N1-F2], which is informative but not generalizable across all patient populations. The broader steroid evidence is also heterogeneous, with some studies reporting superior outcomes for dexamethasone implant in resistant DME and others finding no significant difference in nonresistant DME [N2-F3]. This heterogeneity, plus the need for careful patient selection, indicates that current evidence is still insufficient to support broad routine use. The systematic review explicitly notes that no synthetic evidence exists regarding possible confounding factors affecting the efficacy of anti-VEGF and Ozurdex therapies, and that meta-regression was performed to address this [N2-F3]. That gap remains important.

In conclusion, the guidelines and treatment landscape suggest that refractory DME is managed after anti-VEGF failure, with vitrectomy plus implant being a stepwise option for non-tractional refractory disease [N5-F4][N1-F2]. The broader evidence supports using dexamethasone implant as an adjunct, particularly in resistant DME or in combination with anti-VEGF, but also highlights the need for careful patient selection and caution because the evidence is limited and heterogeneous [N2-F3][N5-F4]. The main gaps are the lack of large randomized trials, the role of confounding factors, and the need to better define which patients are most likely to benefit from vitrectomy plus implant versus other treatments [N2-F3][N1-F2].

## Integrated final answer: clinical evidence supporting vitrectomy plus dexamethasone implant for refractory diabetic macular edema

### 1) What the evidence actually shows

The overall clinical evidence supports the use of **pars plana vitrectomy combined with dexamethasone implant** in **refractory diabetic macular edema**, but the support is **stronger in refractory than in routine DME** and **more limited than for first-line anti-VEGF therapy**.

#### Direct evidence for vitrectomy plus dexamethasone implant
The clearest direct evidence is a **3-year retrospective interventional study** of 43 eyes of 39 patients with **non-tractional refractory diabetic macular edema** treated with **vitrectomy combined with intraoperative dexamethasone implantation** [N1-F2]. The study followed patients for **at least 3 years** and defined refractory DME as DME that continued for more than 6 months despite repeated non-surgical treatments, including anti-VEGF therapy, in the absence of traction force on OCT [N1-F2]. In this study, the surgery was performed by a single surgeon using a 23-gauge vitrectomy system, and the implant was placed at the end of the operation [N1-F2].

Other direct evidence includes reports that **vitrectomy combined with intraoperative dexamethasone implantation provides satisfactory long-term clinical outcomes for non-tractional refractory DME** [N3-R2], and that **vitrectomy combined with intraoperative dexamethasone implant may be safe and effective in treating DME, especially tractional DME** [N3-R1]. This suggests that the combination has been studied in both **non-tractional refractory DME** and **tractional DME**.

#### Primary outcomes reported
The main outcomes reported in the direct evidence are consistent with standard DME outcomes:
- **Best corrected visual acuity (BCVA)**: the 3-year non-tractional refractory DME study showed improvement in BCVA [N5-F4].
- **Central macular thickness (CMT)**: the same study reported improvement in central macular thickness [N5-F4].
- **Central subfield thickness**: the direct evidence also supports the use of OCT-based central subfield measurements, though the specific values in the provided branch reports are more directly tied to CMT than to central subfield thickness alone [N1-F2][N5-F4].
- **CRT and CMT measures**: the broader field evidence shows that dexamethasone implant studies commonly report **BCVA, CRT, and CMT**, with follow-up at 1, 3, and 6 months post-implant [N6-R5]. While not the vitrectomy-plus-DEX studies themselves, these outcomes are directly relevant to the clinical context of the procedure.

#### Sample size, follow-up duration, and inclusion/exclusion criteria
The strongest direct study had **43 eyes** of 39 patients with **non-tractional refractory DME**, and the follow-up was **at least 3 years** [N1-F2]. It excluded patients with:
- active proliferative diabetic retinopathy,
- prior vitreoretinal surgery,
- evidence of any other past or concomitant retinal disease,
- and those lost to follow-up before 3 years [N1-F2].

It also excluded patients with vitreomacular traction or epiretinal membrane on OCT, ensuring that the population was specifically **non-tractional refractory DME** [N1-F2]. The broader search result on vitrectomy combined with intraoperative dexamethasone implantation also notes that the study was a **retrospective interventional study** of **consecutive patients** with non-tractional refractory DME followed for **at least 3 years** [N1-F2]. This makes the evidence **more informative for refractory disease than for routine DME**.

### 2) How dexamethasone implant compares with other intravitreal steroids

The evidence for dexamethasone implant as an adjunct in refractory DME is mixed but favorable in resistant disease.

A **systematic review and meta-analysis** of intravitreal dexamethasone implant versus anti-VEGF treatment in DME found that:
- overall, **dexamethasone implant was not inferior to anti-VEGF therapy in nonresistant DME**,
- but in **resistant DME**, it provided **significantly greater VA improvement** and **CRT reduction** than anti-VEGF therapy [N2-F3].

This is important because it positions dexamethasone implant not as a universal replacement for anti-VEGF, but as a potential **adjunct or alternative** when anti-VEGF alone is insufficient.

Another search result suggests that **dexamethasone implant combined with anti-VEGF agents confers superior anatomical outcomes in reducing CMT** compared with anti-VEGF monotherapy in refractory DME [N2-R2]. This indicates that in persistent or recurrent edema, the implant is often used as an **adjunct**, and that combination with anti-VEGF may be more effective than anti-VEGF alone [N2-R2].

A separate search result also notes that **ranibizumab combined with dexamethasone implant** offers **superior clinical efficacy over ranibizumab monotherapy** for RVO-ME, and that this regimen leverages the complementary mechanisms of anti-VEGF and corticosteroid therapy [N2-R3]. Although this is not DME-specific, it reinforces the broader pattern that **combination steroid-anti-VEGF approaches can be more effective than anti-VEGF alone** [N2-R3].

### 3) Effectiveness in patients with persistent or recurrent edema

The evidence supports the use of dexamethasone implant in patients with **persistent or recurrent edema** who have not responded adequately to anti-VEGF therapy.

The key evidence is that dexamethasone implant is more effective than anti-VEGF in **resistant DME** [N2-F3]. The same meta-analysis found that in resistant DME, dexamethasone implant significantly improved VA and reduced CRT [N2-F3]. Another search result suggests that **DEX combined with anti-VEGF agents** provides **superior anatomical outcomes in reducing CMT** compared with anti-VEGF monotherapy in refractory DME [N2-R2]. This is especially relevant to persistent or recurrent edema because it suggests that the implant is used not only as a **first-line steroid** but also as an **adjunct after anti-VEGF failure**.

### 4) Limitations and reasons for retreatment or failure

The evidence also indicates that dexamethasone implant is not a perfect solution and that retreatment or failure can occur.

First, the meta-analysis found that dexamethasone implant was **not inferior to anti-VEGF therapy in nonresistant DME**, which means it is not universally superior and may not be the best choice for all DME patients [N2-F3]. Second, the same review notes that results depend on subgroup definitions and that **heterogeneity in study results and possible confounding factors remain important challenges in DME treatment** [N2-F3]. This suggests that some patients may not benefit and may require further intervention.

A related implication is that **retreatment or failure is likely when the disease is not truly resistant**, when there are other confounding factors, or when the patient does not meet the criteria for refractory disease [N2-F3]. The broader treatment landscape also suggests that **some patients may still not achieve durable benefit** and may need alternative treatments, including vitrectomy plus implant [N2-F3].

### 5) Safety, risks, and patient selection considerations

The safety profile of dexamethasone implant is **mixed but concerning**.

Major complications reported include **endophthalmitis**, **cataract**, **glaucoma**, **retinal detachment**, and **conjunctival hemorrhage** [N4-R2]. A separate source notes that **endophthalmitis following intravitreal DEX implant is uncommon but serious**, and that it is a rare but notable complication of a procedure that is frequent in medical retina practice [N4-R1]. Another search result reports a **low incidence of endophthalmitis after dexamethasone implant**, but **higher than after anti-VEGF**, which further highlights the procedural risk [N4-R3].

In terms of safety signals versus potential benefits, the evidence suggests that the implant may be justified in **refractory cases** where anti-VEGF alone is insufficient, because dexamethasone implant was significantly more effective than anti-VEGF in resistant DME for VA and CRT [N2-F3]. However, the same evidence also shows that **some patients may still not benefit**, and that **endophthalmitis, cataract, and glaucoma** remain real risks [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3].

Patient selection is therefore crucial. The evidence supports using the implant in patients with:
- **persistent or recurrent DME**,
- **refractory DME** after anti-VEGF,
- and where other treatments have failed or are inadequate [N2-F3][N2-R2].

At the same time, the evidence suggests that the implant should be avoided in patients with:
- **active proliferative diabetic retinopathy**,
- **prior vitreoretinal surgery**,
- and other concomitant retinal diseases that could increase surgical risk [N1-F2][N5-F4].

In other words, the strongest safety signal is that **DEX implant is not harmless**, and the strongest benefit signal is that it can help **refractory cases where other treatments have failed** [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N2-F3].

### 6) Context from guidelines and the broader treatment landscape

Current guidelines and the broader treatment landscape frame **refractory diabetic macular edema** as a situation where **anti-VEGF therapy alone is insufficient**, and alternative treatments are considered [N2-F3][N5-F4]. In the non-tractional refractory DME study, vitrectomy with or without ILM peeling is described as a **well-established treatment for DME cases with a tractional component**, while its role for nontractional cases is **unclear** [N5-F4]. This reflects the broader treatment landscape: **vitrectomy is established for tractional DME**, but not clearly established for nontractional refractory DME, and **steroid implants are increasingly used as adjuncts or alternatives when anti-VEGF is inadequate** [N5-F4][N2-F3].

In that context, **vitrectomy plus implant fits into stepwise treatment algorithms** as a more aggressive option for refractory disease. The non-tractional refractory DME study defines refractory DME as DME continuing for more than 6 months despite repeated non-surgical treatments, and treats these patients with **vitrectomy combined with intraoperative dexamethasone implantation** [N1-F2]. This suggests a stepwise approach in which **non-surgical anti-VEGF is tried first**, and then, in refractory cases, **vitrectomy with adjunct steroid implant is considered** [N1-F2].

The broader treatment landscape also includes other intravitreal steroids and combination therapies. The evidence shows that dexamethasone implant is compared with **ranibizumab** and other anti-VEGF agents, and that **combination with anti-VEGF can provide superior anatomical outcomes in refractory DME** [N2-R2][N2-R3]. This means that **vitrectomy plus implant should be understood within a larger steroid-anti-VEGF combination framework**, rather than as an isolated option [N2-R2][N2-R3]. The search result also notes that **corticosteroids including intravitreal implants have played a critical role in the treatment of DME** [N5-R4], reinforcing that steroids are part of the broader treatment toolbox.

### 7) Limitations of current evidence and gaps in knowledge

The limitations of current evidence are substantial.

First, the direct evidence on **vitrectomy plus dexamethasone implant** is **limited in number and mostly retrospective or observational** [N1-F2]. The strongest direct study had **43 eyes** of 39 patients with **non-tractional refractory DME**, and the follow-up was **at least 3 years** [N1-F2], which is informative but not generalizable across all patient populations.

Second, the broader steroid evidence is **heterogeneous**, with some studies reporting superior outcomes for dexamethasone implant in resistant DME and others finding no significant difference in nonresistant DME [N2-F3]. This heterogeneity, plus the need for careful patient selection, indicates that **current evidence is still insufficient to support broad routine use** [N2-F3].

Third, the evidence also shows that **no synthetic evidence exists regarding possible confounding factors** affecting the efficacy of anti-VEGF and Ozurdex therapies, and that **meta-regression was performed to address this** [N2-F3]. That gap remains important.

Fourth, the evidence for **long-term outcomes and refractory cases** is encouraging, but still limited in scope and design [N3-R2][N3-R1][N1-F2]. The direct evidence supports meaningful anatomical and visual improvement in refractory DME, but the sample sizes and follow-up durations suggest that **larger randomized trials are needed** [N1-F2][N5-F4].

### 8) Bottom line

Clinical evidence supports **vitrectomy combined with dexamethasone implant** in **refractory diabetic macular edema**, but the support is strongest in **refractory rather than routine DME**.

- **Direct evidence**: there is a 3-year retrospective interventional study of 43 eyes with non-tractional refractory DME showing improvement in BCVA and central macular thickness [N1-F2][N5-F4].
- **Dexamethasone implant as an adjunct**: it is more effective than anti-VEGF in resistant DME and can be combined with anti-VEGF for superior anatomical outcomes in refractory DME [N2-F3][N2-R2].
- **Safety and patient selection**: the implant is associated with serious complications such as endophthalmitis, cataract, and glaucoma, so it should be reserved for patients with persistent or recurrent DME who have failed anti-VEGF, and avoided in patients with active PDR or prior vitreoretinal surgery [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N1-F2].
- **Guidelines and treatment landscape**: vitrectomy is established for tractional DME, but not clearly established for nontractional refractory DME; steroid implants are increasingly used as adjuncts after anti-VEGF failure [N5-F4][N2-F3].
- **Limitations**: the evidence is limited, heterogeneous, and mostly retrospective, so larger randomized trials are needed to better define the role of vitrectomy plus implant [N1-F2][N2-F3].

## Final recommendation

For **refractory diabetic macular edema**, the evidence supports **vitrectomy plus dexamethasone implant** as a reasonable **stepwise or salvage option**, especially in patients who have failed anti-VEGF therapy and have persistent or recurrent edema [N1-F2][N2-F3]. However, it should be used **selectively**, with careful attention to safety, patient selection, and the limitations of current evidence [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N2-F3].

The direct evidence base is relatively small but notable. The follow-up was at least 3 years, and the surgery was performed by a single surgeon using a 23-gauge vitrectomy system with removal of the ILM around 2 disc diameters from the fovea in some cases [N1-F2]. The study explicitly states that it was a retrospective interventional study of consecutive patients treated with vitrectomy combined with intravitreal dexamethasone implantation and followed up for at least 3 years [N1-F2]. This is the clearest direct evidence that vitrectomy was combined with dexamethasone implant in DME.

Another relevant direct source is the search result describing “vitrectomy combined with intraoperative dexamethasone implantation provides satisfactory long-term clinical outcomes for non-tractional refractory DME” [N3-R2]. That excerpt also notes that eyes with DME that were successfully treated by vitrectomy combined with dexamethasone implantation and remained stable for a year were reported in the literature [N3-R2]. This supports the existence of direct studies in refractory DME, but it is not a full study report. A later search result similarly says that vitrectomy combined with intraoperative dexamethasone implant may be safe and effective in treating DME, especially tractional DME [N3-R1]. This expands the direct evidence to tractional DME as well as non-tractional refractory DME.

On outcomes, the 3-year study on non-tractional refractory DME reported improvement in central macular thickness and BCVA. The mean central macular thickness improved from 413.1 ± 84.4 to 291.3 ± 57.6 μm at two years, and mean logMAR BCVA improved from 0.6 ± 0.2 to 0.2 ± 0.1 [N5-F4]. This is important because it shows that vitrectomy plus implant can produce meaningful anatomical and visual improvement in refractory DME, but the benefit appears to vary by baseline features.

The evidence also includes direct study design and outcome measures. The 3-year vitrectomy-plus-DEX study reported preoperative and postoperative BCVA and OCT scans at 6, 12, and 24 months [N5-F4]. While these are not the vitrectomy-plus-DEX studies themselves, they confirm the standard outcome measures used in the field and support the plausibility of the reported results. The 2020 study excerpt also notes that dexamethasone implant can reduce CRT and improve visual acuity, with a peak effect at 8 to 13 weeks after implant [N6-R4], which is consistent with the expected pharmacokinetic profile of the implant.

Sample size, follow-up duration, and inclusion/exclusion criteria are therefore varied. The strongest direct study had 43 eyes of 39 patients with non-tractional refractory DME and at least 3 years of follow-up [N1-F2]. The non-tractional refractory DME study excluded patients with active proliferative diabetic retinopathy, prior vitreoretinal surgery, evidence of any other past or concomitant retinal disease, and those lost to follow-up before 3 years [N1-F2]. The search result for vitrectomy combined with intraoperative dexamethasone implantation also notes that the study was a retrospective interventional study of consecutive patients with non-tractional refractory DME followed for at least 3 years [N1-F2]. In contrast, the search result on vitrectomy combined with intraoperative dexamethasone implant in tractional DME is more general in phrasing, but still indicates direct clinical use [N3-R1].

Overall, the direct evidence shows that vitrectomy plus dexamethasone implant has been studied in both non-tractional refractory DME and tractional DME, with the strongest direct evidence being a 3-year retrospective interventional study of 43 eyes with non-tractional refractory DME [N1-F2]. The primary outcomes included BCVA, central macular thickness, and OCT measures, and the study found meaningful improvement in anatomical and visual outcomes [N5-F4]. The inclusion/exclusion criteria were fairly restrictive, emphasizing refractory disease without traction force, exclusion of active PDR, prior vitreoretinal surgery, and other concomitant retinal diseases [N1-F2]. The evidence is therefore directly supportive of vitrectomy plus dexamethasone implant in refractory DME, but the sample sizes and follow-up durations suggest that the field still relies on limited, mostly retrospective or observational studies rather than large randomized trials [N1-F2][N5-F4].

The main outcomes reported in the direct evidence are consistent with standard DME outcomes:

The strongest direct study had **43 eyes** of 39 patients with **non-tractional refractory DME**, and the follow-up was **at least 3 years** [N1-F2]. It excluded patients with:

The evidence for dexamethasone implant as an adjunct in refractory DME is mixed but favorable in resistant disease.

A **systematic review and meta-analysis** of intravitreal dexamethasone implant versus anti-VEGF treatment in DME found that:
- overall, **dexamethasone implant was not inferior to anti-VEGF therapy in nonresistant DME**,
